cards.front: Why do human geneticists use pedigrees instead of controlled crosses?
cards.back: Humans cannot be set up in crosses, so geneticists work backwards from existing families.
cards.quote: Human geneticists cannot set up crosses, so they work backwards from existing families.

cards.front: In pedigree logic, what does a fitting prediction show, and what can a single contradiction do?
cards.back: A fit supports a model but does not prove it. One contradiction can rule the model out, within the stated scope.
cards.why: The scope is five single-gene models, full penetrance, no new mutation and correct relationships.
cards.quote: A model that fits is supported, not proved.

cards.front: In a pedigree, a filled symbol means {{c1::affected}} by the condition named in the key.
cards.back: A diagonal slash marks someone who has died.
cards.quote: A filled symbol means affected by the condition named in the key; a diagonal slash marks someone who has died.

cards.front: What do a square, a circle and a diamond mean in the 2022 revised pedigree standard?
cards.back: Square: man or boy. Circle: woman or girl. Diamond: nonbinary person or someone whose sex or gender is not specified.
cards.quote: a square is a man or boy, a circle is a woman or girl, and a diamond is a nonbinary person or someone whose sex or gender is not specified.

cards.front: In a pedigree, how is a person labelled as II-3, and what does an arrow mark?
cards.back: Roman numerals label generations and people are numbered left to right, so II-3 is the third person in generation II. An arrow marks the proband.
cards.quote: Roman numerals label generations, and people are numbered left to right, so II-3 identifies one person.

cards.front: The {{c1::proband}} is the person through whom the family came to attention.
cards.back: Shown by an arrow on the pedigree.
cards.quote: An arrow marks the proband, through whom the family came to attention.

cards.front: A pedigree shows two partners joined by a double horizontal line. What does it record, and what does it not record?
cards.back: It records consanguinity: the partners are related by descent. It does not record that both carry the allele.
cards.why: Shared ancestry raises the chance of carrying the same rare allele but proves nothing about genotype.
cards.quote: A double partner line marks consanguinity: the partners are related by descent, as first cousins are.

cards.front: A {{c1::carrier}} is heterozygous for a recessive allele and usually does not show the trait.
cards.quote: A carrier is heterozygous for a recessive allele and usually does not show the trait.

cards.front: Under the simple model, what is the signature of autosomal dominant inheritance, and what observation contradicts it?
cards.back: One copy is enough, so the trait usually appears in successive generations and in both sexes. An affected child with two unaffected parents contradicts it.
cards.quote: The trait usually appears in successive generations and both sexes; father-to-son transmission is possible.

cards.front: An affected heterozygote and an unaffected partner give each child a {{c1::1/2}} allele risk under autosomal dominant inheritance.
cards.quote: An affected heterozygote and unaffected partner give each child a 1/2 allele risk.

cards.front: Why do autosomal recessive cases often cluster among siblings with few affected relatives elsewhere?
cards.back: Unaffected carrier parents can have affected children of either sex, so affected people concentrate in one sibship.
cards.quote: Unaffected carrier parents can have affected children of either sex, so cases often cluster among siblings, with few affected relatives elsewhere.

cards.front: Two parents with the same autosomal recessive trait have an unaffected child. What does this rule out, and what is the qualification?
cards.back: It contradicts autosomal recessive inheritance only if the same gene causes both parents' trait.
cards.why: Different genes can cause the same phenotype, as in recessive deafness.
cards.quote: Two affected parents have an unaffected child, if the same gene causes both parents' trait.

cards.front: Two deaf parents have a child with normal hearing. Does this rule out recessive inheritance of deafness in that family?
cards.back: No, not by itself. Different genes can cause deafness, so this contradicts recessive inheritance only if the same gene causes both parents' trait.
cards.quote: Recessive deafness shows why that row's qualification matters: different genes can cause deafness, so two deaf parents can have a hearing child.

cards.front: Why are affected males much more common than affected females in X-linked recessive traits?
cards.back: A male has one X, so one copy can affect him.
cards.why: A woman needs two copies, though heterozygous women can show signs partly through X-inactivation.
cards.quote: Affected men are much more common than affected women.

cards.front: How does an X-linked recessive allele pass from an affected man to his grandsons?
cards.back: He passes it through carrier daughters, who pass it to half their sons.
cards.quote: An affected man passes the allele through carrier daughters to half their sons.

cards.front: An affected father has an unaffected daughter. Under full penetrance and no new mutation, which of the five models does this one observation rule out?
cards.back: Only X-linked dominant. Every daughter receives her father's X, so she would be affected. The other four models allow an unaffected daughter.
cards.quote: An affected father passes the allele to every daughter and no son.

cards.front: In X-linked dominant inheritance, what does an affected heterozygous mother pass to her children?
cards.back: The allele goes to half her children, of either sex.
cards.quote: An affected heterozygous mother passes it to half her children of either sex.

cards.front: An affected man and an unaffected woman have three daughters and three sons. All daughters are affected and no son is. Under full penetrance, which mode fits best, and why?
cards.back: X-linked dominant. A father gives his X to every daughter and his Y to every son, so all daughters and no sons are affected.
cards.quote: An affected father passes the allele to every daughter and no son.

cards.front: Which observation rules out X-linked recessive inheritance, and what condition must hold?
cards.back: Demonstrated father-to-son transmission. An affected father-son pair excludes it only if the mother carries no copy.
cards.why: A son gets his father's Y, so the X-linked allele could only come from his mother.
cards.quote: An affected father-son pair establishes this only if the mother carries no copy.

cards.front: What is the pattern of mitochondrial inheritance, and what observation rules it out?
cards.back: An affected mother can have affected children of both sexes; an affected father transmits the trait to none. Transmission from an affected father rules it out.
cards.quote: An affected mother can have affected children of both sexes; an affected father transmits the trait to none.

cards.front: Human mitochondrial DNA normally comes from the {{c1::mother}}.
cards.quote: Human mitochondrial DNA normally comes from the mother.

cards.front: Why do many mitochondrial diseases follow Mendelian patterns instead of maternal inheritance?
cards.back: Mitochondrial DNA encodes only a handful of respiratory-chain subunits; most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded.
cards.quote: most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded, so many mitochondrial diseases instead follow Mendelian patterns.

cards.front: Why is "the trait skips a generation" not proof of recessive inheritance?
cards.back: Reduced penetrance can make a dominant allele appear to skip a generation.
cards.quote: reduced penetrance can make a dominant allele appear to skip.

cards.front: A man is unaffected and his sister has an autosomal recessive disorder. Both parents are unaffected. With full penetrance and no new mutation, what is his carrier probability?
cards.back: 2/3. The affected sister makes both parents Aa. Aa x Aa gives AA, Aa, aA, aa at 1/4 each. Being unaffected removes aa, leaving 3 outcomes, 2 of them carriers.
cards.quote: Her affected brother shows that both parents are carriers, Aa.

cards.front: Why is the carrier probability of an unaffected sibling of an affected person 2/3 and not 1/2?
cards.back: 1/2 is the carrier probability before the phenotype is known. His unaffected phenotype removes the aa outcome, so the carriers are 2 of the 3 remaining equal outcomes.
cards.quote: The tempting 1/2 was her carrier probability before her unaffected phenotype removed one outcome.

cards.front: A woman's brother has cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive); she and her parents are unaffected. Her partner has no family history, with an assumed carrier frequency of 1/25. What is the probability their first child is affected?
cards.back: 1/150. She is a carrier with probability 2/3, her partner with 1/25, and two carriers pass a at 1/4: 2/3 x 1/25 x 1/4 = 2/300 = 1/150.
cards.why: The 1/25 is an exercise assumption, not a universal figure.
cards.quote: Therefore P(affected child) = 2/3 x 1/25 x 1/4 = 2/300 = 1/150

cards.front: A woman's mother is a known carrier of a fully penetrant X-linked recessive allele and her father is unaffected. What is her prior carrier probability, and why?
cards.back: 1/2. Her father gave her a normal X, and her mother passed one of her two X chromosomes.
cards.quote: Her unaffected father gave her a normal X and her mother one of two X chromosomes, so her prior is 1/2 carrier and 1/2 not carrier.
cards.section: Updating with evidence: Bayes and unaffected sons

cards.front: In Bayes' rule applied to a pedigree, how do you combine a prior and a likelihood for each hypothesis?
cards.back: Multiply each prior (the weight before the evidence) by its likelihood (the chance of the evidence under that hypothesis), then normalize the weights.
cards.quote: Multiply each prior (the weight before the evidence) by its likelihood (the chance of the evidence under that hypothesis)
cards.section: Updating with evidence: Bayes and unaffected sons

cards.front: An untested woman with a 1/2 prior of carrying an X-linked recessive allele has two unaffected sons. Does her carrier probability rise or fall, and what is it?
cards.back: It falls to 1/5. Carrier: 1/2 x 1/4 = 1/8. Not carrier: 1/2 x 1 = 1/2. Posterior = (1/8) / (1/8 + 1/2) = 1/5.
cards.why: Two unaffected sons are likelier if she is not a carrier.
cards.quote: Under the same model, her next son's affected risk is 1/5 x 1/2 = 1/10.
cards.section: Updating with evidence: Bayes and unaffected sons

cards.front: A woman whose mother is a known carrier of a fully penetrant X-linked recessive allele has had two unaffected sons and is now updated to a 1/5 carrier probability. What is the risk that her next son is affected?
cards.back: 1/10. She carries with probability 1/5, and a carrier mother passes the allele to a son with probability 1/2: 1/5 x 1/2 = 1/10.
cards.quote: Under the same model, her next son's affected risk is 1/5 x 1/2 = 1/10.
cards.section: Updating with evidence: Bayes and unaffected sons

cards.front: In the updating example, prior odds 1 : 1 became posterior odds 1 : 4 after two unaffected sons. What explains the factor of four?
cards.back: The evidence is four times likelier if she is not a carrier: likelihood 1 versus 1/4.
cards.quote: Prior odds of 1 : 1 become posterior odds of 1 : 4, because the evidence is four times likelier if she is not a carrier.
cards.section: Updating with evidence: Bayes and unaffected sons

cards.front: An autosomal dominant allele has 80% penetrance. A heterozygous parent and a parent without the allele have a child. What is the probability the child is affected?
cards.back: 0.40. The child inherits the allele with probability 1/2 and shows the condition with probability 0.8: 0.5 x 0.8 = 0.40.
cards.quote: Genotype may not predict one visible phenotype.

cards.front: Why might a young unaffected child of a parent with Huntington disease still carry the allele?
cards.back: Huntington disease is dominant, but symptoms usually begin in adulthood, so a young child can carry the allele and be unaffected.
cards.quote: Huntington disease is dominant, but symptoms usually begin in adulthood, so a young unaffected child of an affected parent may carry the allele.

cards.front: In HTT, what CAG repeat counts are usually described as reduced penetrance and as full penetrance?
cards.back: About 36 to 39 repeats: reduced penetrance. 40 or more: full penetrance.
cards.quote: Penetrance also depends on CAG repeat length in HTT: about 36 to 39 repeats is usually described as reduced penetrance, and 40 or more as full penetrance.

cards.front: {{c1::Variable expressivity}} means the same genotype produces different clinical pictures.
cards.quote: Variable expressivity means the same genotype produces different clinical pictures.

cards.front: A child with a dominant disorder has two unaffected parents. This looks like a contradiction of autosomal dominant inheritance. Give an explanation that does not rule the model out.
cards.back: A new pathogenic variant can produce a dominant disorder in a child of unaffected parents. Germline mosaicism in a parent is another route.
cards.quote: A new pathogenic variant can produce a dominant disorder in a child of unaffected parents, which looks exactly like the observation that rules out autosomal dominant inheritance.

cards.front: In germline mosaicism, a parent carries a variant in only some cells, including some {{c1::sperm or eggs}}.
cards.quote: In germline mosaicism, a parent carries a variant in only some cells, including some sperm or eggs.

cards.front: In a study of 58 families with one affected child and an apparently new variant, how often was recurrence risk low, and what did parental mosaicism change?
cards.back: Estimated recurrence was below 0.1% in 35 families; 5 families had parental mosaicism associated with higher risk, and three fathers had the variant in 5.6 to 12.1% of sperm DNA.
cards.quote: 5 had parental mosaicism associated with higher risk, and three fathers had the variant in 5.6 to 12.1% of sperm DNA.

cards.front: What is heteroplasmy, and why does it make mitochondrial severity vary between siblings?
cards.back: A cell contains both normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA. A mother can transmit different proportions to different children, so severity varies and some may be unaffected.
cards.quote: A mother can transmit different proportions to different children, so severity varies and some children may be unaffected.

cards.front: Two carrier parents of an autosomal recessive allele have two children. What is the probability that neither is affected, and what does it imply for judging the model?
cards.back: (3/4)^2 = 9/16, more than half the time. Seeing no affected child is not enough to reject autosomal recessive inheritance.
cards.quote: Small families can look as though nothing is inherited.

cards.front: Whole-genome blood sequences from 11,035 trios showed seven children with a paternal-like mitochondrial signal at 5 to 25% of reads. All seven fathers and children also shared a mitochondrial-derived insert in a nuclear chromosome. What do these data support?
cards.back: An inherited nuclear insert can mimic paternal mitochondrial DNA. Apparent exceptions to maternal inheritance need molecular checks.
cards.quote: Apparent exceptions also need molecular checks: among 11,035 trios, all seven apparent paternal mitochondrial signals were explained by a mitochondrial-derived nuclear insert shared by father and child.

cards.front: An affected woman has five affected children. Her affected son has three unaffected children. Which person's children best discriminate mitochondrial from X-linked dominant inheritance, and why?
cards.back: The affected son. He transmits no mitochondrial DNA, so three unaffected children fit mitochondrial inheritance. Under fully penetrant X-linked dominant inheritance every daughter would be affected, so the data exclude it only if at least one is a daughter.
cards.quote: He transmits no mitochondrial DNA, so three unaffected children fit mitochondrial inheritance.

cards.front: Under X-linked dominant inheritance, what is the probability that a heterozygous mother has five affected children, and how does it bear on choosing between that model and mitochondrial inheritance?
cards.back: (1/2)^5 = 1/32: possible but unlikely. A mother transmits mitochondria to every child, so five affected children fits mitochondrial inheritance more easily, though it does not exclude X-linked dominant.
cards.quote: under X-linked dominant inheritance, five affected children of a heterozygous mother has probability (1/2)^5 = 1/32: possible but unlikely.

cards.front: In a family with an affected mother and variable severity, can variable severity decide between mitochondrial and X-linked dominant inheritance?
cards.back: No. Heteroplasmy gives children different mutant fractions, and X-inactivation can vary an X-linked dominant phenotype in women. Both models fit.
cards.quote: Variable severity fits both models, so it cannot decide between them.

cards.front: Design a molecular test to support the mitochondrial model in a family with variable severity.
cards.back: Sequence affected and unaffected relatives, look for a variant confined to the maternal line, and measure heteroplasmy in several tissues. Heteroplasmy tracking severity, with the variant absent from the affected son's children, would support the mitochondrial model.
cards.quote: Heteroplasmy tracking severity, with the variant absent from the son's children, would support the mitochondrial model.
